terms.gloss: a statesman, a man in public life
terms.grammar: noun phrase; for a woman, fēmina cīvīlis (Traupman 180)
evidence: Quint. 11.1.35: at vir cīvīlis vērēque sapiēns
terms.comment: Quintilian’s phrase for the statesman, the Greek πολιτικός (Lewis & Short, s.v. cīvīlis); Traupman gives it for both politician and statesman. It is a word of praise: for the trade of seeking office see ambitiō (politics) and candidātus (apply for). Morgan–Owens calls an elected politician magistrātus (see official).
Classically only an adjective, of the state or of political philosophy (Cic.; Lewis & Short); as a noun for a politician it is modern. Andresian also gives the feminine polītica.

phrases.latin: at vir cīvīlis vērēque sapiēns, quī sē nōn ōtiōsīs disputātiōnibus, sed administrātiōnī reī pūblicae dēdiderit
phrases.english: but the statesman, the man who is wise in fact, who has given himself not to idle debate but to the running of the state

sources: Lewis & Short: civilis · Lewis & Short: vir
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 180.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. politician.
Quintilian 11.1.35, checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
